## Abstract

The purpose of this project is to investigate whether Ireland is caring for its historic fairy habitats. Because fairies are notorious for obstructing data collection and interfering with computer calculations, there is very little data available on fairy habitats and their preservation. This is a two-part project, where we first determine where fairies prefer to live, and then assess whether their preferred habitat is flourishing. Data collected (with much sacrifice) on the location of fairy barrows (homes) will be converted into a density layer to determine where fairy barrows are most densely clustered. Next, land cover data from 1990 will be compared to the barrow density to determine which habitat fairies prefer. To test whether fairies cluster near stone circles, rather than a particular habitat, a  will be done on the average distance of fairy barrows from nearby stone circles. The preferred habitat for stone circles will also be noted. Finally, land cover data from 2018 will be compared to the 1990 dataset, to produce a change matrix, and identify whether Irish fairy habitat remains intact.

## Introduction
Ireland's human inhabitants share the land with a cryptic, fickle, whimsical species known as the Aes Sídhe. They are also known as the Wee Folk, the Good People, the Fair Folk, or,  most generally, fairies. The ancient name, Aes Sídhe, means *folk of the fairy mounds,* referring to the mounds the fairies live in. These mounds, also known as *barrows,* are found throughout Ireland, and are regarded with superstition and reverence. This caution is well-founded, as those who disturb or damage these mounds are punished with extensive bad luck and guaranteed disaster. 

Unfortunately, the secreteive (and vengeful) nature of the Folk makes them difficult to study. As a result, modern researchers know very little about their preferred habitats, and the growing climate crisis is leading to worries about habitat suitability for Ireland's Good Neighbors (another moniker). Restless fairies are prone to violent outbursts, which presents a danger to Ireland's human inhabitants. 

This study will use the little data we have to determine if fairies have a preferred habitat, and extend that finding to assess whether Ireland is properly preserving that preferred habitat. If the author survives to the completion of this study, it may offer important insights about the future of humanity's relationship with our fairy neighbors. 

The hypotheses tested in this study are as follows: (ok so we need a way to say "yeah this was proven wrong, so we pivoted!")

Null Hypothesis: Fairies in the Republic of Ireland display no significant clustering in home locations, indicating no preference in habitat.

Hypothesis 1: Fairies in the Republic of Ireland prefer forested habitats.

Hypothesis 2: Fairies in the Republic of Ireland prefer to live near stone circles.

Hypothesis 3: Stone circles were built in a certain habitat, reflecting the nature of the fairy realm on the other side.

(fairies prefer to live in separate habitats than their hunting habitats, indicating a deep misunderstanding in fairy ecology)

barrows: "Barrows are typically defined as circular enclosures of earth and/or stone, often featuring a bank and ditch, though there are also examples without these features, consisting only of a simple mound. The interior of a barrow can take the form of a flat platform or shallow depression, but the most common type found in Ireland is the ring barrow. These barrows feature a low mound that rises gradually from the enclosing ditch and have an overall diameter of 15 to 25 meters."

stone circles: "These circles are characterised by the presence of standing stones, typically made of sandstone or quartz, that are arranged in a circular pattern. Stone circles can range in size from a few metres to over 100 metres in diameter, and they are thought to have served a variety of religious, cultural, and astronomical purposes."

## Methodology
To test our hypotheses, the locations of fairy barrows will be compared to land cover data from 1990 to determine whether fairies prefer a certain habitat (first-order clustering). To test whether fairies cluster near stone circles (second-order clustering), rather than a particular habitat, we will compare the average distance of fairy barrows to nearby stone circles. The preferred habitat for stone circle construction will also be tested with the same land cover data, as we have very little information about fairy habits. If any preferred habitats are found, land cover data from 2018 will be compared to the 1990 dataset to produce a change matrix, and identify whether fairy habitat in the Repulic of Ireland remains intact. 

# Study Environment Preparation

This study was conducted using R, with the packages tidyverse, sf, mapview, spatstat, stars, rnaturalearth, terra, tidyterra, and pbapply.

The Coordinate Reference System (CRS) for this study is the Irish Transverse Mercator (ITM) projection, with EPSG code 2157. All data is reprojected or transformed into this CRS for calculations and visualizations. (cite)

```{r}
#| label: itinialiigjgjg
library(tidyverse) |> suppressPackageStartupMessages()
library(sf) |> suppressPackageStartupMessages()
library(mapview) |> suppressPackageStartupMessages()
library(spatstat) |> suppressPackageStartupMessages()
library(stars) |> suppressPackageStartupMessages()
library(rnaturalearth) |> suppressPackageStartupMessages()
library(terra) |> suppressPackageStartupMessages()
library(tidyterra) |> suppressPackageStartupMessages()
library(pbapply) |> suppressPackageStartupMessages()
set.seed(6805)
```

# Fairy Point Data Preparation
Barrows and Stone Circles data were collected from the Irish Archaeology website, downloaded in kml format from the associated Interactive Google Map, and converted to CSV. The CSV was also cleaned in Microsoft Excel to retain all downloaded information in a usable format for the sf library. (cite) Metadata for these datasets can be found in the Appendix(link?). 

```{r}
#| label: barrows data prep

barrows_df <- read_csv('data/raw/barrows.csv')
barrows_df <- barrows_df |> select(townland, class_code, latitude, longitude) |> mutate(type = "barrow")

barrows_sf <- barrows_df |> sf::st_as_sf(
  coords=c("longitude","latitude"),
  crs=4326) #projected to work with mapview, will reproject to Irish Transverse Mercator (ITM) (EPSG:2157)
  #also the land cover data is epsg 4326

mapview(head(barrows_sf,100)) #showing the first 100 points
head(barrows_sf)

```

```{r}
#| label: circles data prep

stone_circles_df <- read_csv('data/raw/stone-circles.csv')
stone_circles_df <- stone_circles_df |> select(townland, class_code, latitude, longitude) |> mutate(type = "stone circle")

stone_circles_sf <- stone_circles_df |> sf::st_as_sf(
  coords=c("longitude","latitude"),
  crs=4326) #projected to work with mapview, will reproject to Irish Transverse Mercator (ITM) (EPSG:2157)
  #also the land cover data is epsg 4326

mapview(head(stone_circles_sf,100)) #showing the first 100 points
head(stone_circles_sf)

```

```{r}
#| label: combiningn them for some reason, probably visualization help
fairies_sf <- rbind(barrows_sf, stone_circles_sf)
fairies_sf <- fairies_sf |> sf::st_transform(2157)

fairies_map <- mapview(fairies_sf, zcol="type")

```

The observation window for this study is the Natural Earth Data Republic of Ireland sf object at 1:10m resolution. All calculations are constrained to the bounds of this polygon. (cite)

```{r}
#| label: ireland observation window

ireland <- ne_countries(country = "ireland", scale="large") |> select(name,geometry)
ireland <- ireland |> sf::st_transform(2157)
mapview(ireland) + fairies_map

```

Each of the point layers were converted into a spatstat ppp (planar point pattern) object and plotted inside the Ireland observation window for the remainder of the calculations.

```{r}
#| label: barrows ppp 1
barrows_sf <- barrows_sf |> sf::st_transform(2157)
#some of the points are outside my ireland shapefile, so I am going to remove them (since I have thousands)
barrows_sf <- barrows_sf[st_within(barrows_sf, ireland, sparse = FALSE), ] 
barrows_ppp <- as.ppp(barrows_sf, W=as.owin(ireland)) 
barrows_ppp |> sf::st_as_sf() |> ggplot() +
    geom_sf() +
    theme_classic()

```


# Land Cover Data Preparation

Land cover data from 1990 and 2018 was collected from the EU Copernicus component of the European Union's space program. It is produced by the Coordination of Information on the Environment (CORINE) program, which provides a uniform, continent-wide land cover inventory with 44 thematic classes called the CORINE Land Cover product. (cite a few things) Full metadata of the 44 classes and their associated reclassification can be found in the Appendix(link?).

```{r}
#| label: reading in the rasters againnnn

temp_dir <- tempdir() #temporary directory for working
zip_file_path <- "data/raw/Rasters.zip" #path to raster
unzip(zipfile = zip_file_path, exdir = temp_dir) #unzipping into temp directory

# 1990 dataset
tiff_file_path_1990 <- file.path(temp_dir, "Rasters/U2000_CLC1990_V2020_20u1/U2000_CLC1990_V2020_20u1/U2000_CLC1990_V2020_20u1.tif")
lc_1990 <- rast(tiff_file_path_1990)



# 2018 dataset
tiff_file_path_2018 <- file.path(temp_dir, "Rasters/U2018_CLC2018_V2020_20u1/U2018_CLC2018_V2020_20u1/U2018_CLC2018_V2020_20u1.tif")
lc_2018 <- rast(tiff_file_path_2018)



```

```{r}
#| label: reclassification 1990 2 at the beginning
rclmat <- matrix(c(1, 11, 1,
                   11.999, 22, 2,
                   22.999, 25, 3,
                   25.999, 27, 4,
                   27.999, 29, 3,
                   29.999, 34, 5,
                   34.999, 39, 6,
                   39.999, 44, 7
                   ), ncol=3, byrow=TRUE) #decimals so that it catches all possible values

rc_lc_1990 <- classify(lc_1990, rclmat, include.lowest=TRUE)

```


Turning the classified raster into polygons so we can start doing the simulations

```{r}
#| label: raster into polygons
lc_poly_1990 <- as.polygons(rc_lc_1990)

  group_by(U2000_CLC1990_V2020_20u1) |>
  summarise()

lc_poly_sf <- st_intersection(lc_poly_sf, ireland) #clipping the polygons so the borders are the same as my viewing window

mapview(lc_poly_sf, zcol = "U2000_CLC1990_V2020_20u1")

```



Generating test statistic!
```{r}
#| label: barrow counts by habitat
#making lc into a tesselation
lc_list <- split(lc_poly_sf, lc_poly_sf$U2000_CLC1990_V2020_20u1) #grabbing individual polygons
lc_tiles <- lapply(lc_list, as.owin) #each one as a window

#tesselation of the polygon windows
lc_tess <- tess(tiles = lc_tiles)

#now the test statistic
obs_barrow_counts <- quadratcount(barrows_ppp, tess=lc_tess) |> as.vector()
names(obs_barrow_counts) <- c("Dense Human Habitat", "Human Agriculture", "Forests", "Grass and Shrublands", "Rocky, Barren, or Snowy", "Wetlands", "Water Bodies")
obs_barrow_counts <- obs_barrow_counts |> as_tibble_row()
```

The test statistic: Referencing the literature, it is believed that fairies prefer forested habitats, which offer readily available hollow trees, babbling streams, and mossy grottos. Our first hypothesis, therefore, is that fairies prefer to make their homes in forests.

```{r}
obs_barrow_counts
```


habitat 'intensity', which gives the proportional probability of any point existing in each habitat type (based on area)

#| label: habitat intensity function
tile_areas <- sapply(lc_tiles, area.owin) #the area of each tile
tile_probs <- tile_areas / sum(tile_areas) #getting the proportions

habitat_prob_intensity <- function(x, y) { #intensity function for probability of points being in each habitat
  sapply(seq_along(lc_tiles), function(i) {
    inside.owin(x, y, lc_tiles[[i]]) * tile_probs[i]
  }) |> rowSums()
}


```{r}
#new habitat prob intensity, to try and make this run faster
tile_areas <- sapply(lc_tiles, area.owin) #the area of each tile
tile_probs <- tile_areas / sum(tile_areas) #getting the proportions

habitat_prob_intensity <- function(x, y) {
  coords <- cbind(x, y)
  cell_vals <- terra::extract(rc_lc_1990, coords)[,1] #pulls out the habitat value the point lands on top of
  cell_vals[is.na(cell_vals) | is.nan(cell_vals) | cell_vals < 1 | cell_vals > length(tile_probs)] <- 1 #prevent error by keeping everything in range

  probs <- tile_probs[cell_vals] #assigning the probabilties
  
  probs[is.na(probs)] <- 0 #preventing errors with NA by making them 0
  return(probs)
}
```

This is what I ran to do the monte carlo simulations. I never want to run that again, but here is the code
OK and I do have to run this again and save sims_list so that we have the points for the distance calculation, unfortunately

```{r}
library('pbapply')
#Now we are running 999 simulations wahoooo

compute_quadrat_counts <- function(sim_ppp) { #making a function to apply to all the sims
  sim_counts <- quadratcount(sim_ppp, tess=lc_tess) |> as.vector()
  names(sim_counts) <- c("Dense Human Habitat", "Human Agriculture", "Forests", "Grass and Shrublands", "Rocky, Barren, or Snowy", "Wetlands", "Water Bodies")
  return(sim_counts)
}

gen_sims_ppp <- function(num_sims) { #function to generate 999 ppp simulations
  barrows_sims <- spatstat.random::rpoint(
    n = num_barrows,
    f = habitat_prob_intensity,
    win = barrows_ppp$window,
    nsim = num_sims
  )
  return(barrows_sims)
}

sims_list <- gen_sims_ppp(999) #simulations
sims_habitat_counts <- pbapply::pblapply(sims_list, FUN=compute_quadrat_counts) #apply counts function, with a progress bar from pbapply
full_count_df <- as_tibble(sims_habitat_counts) |> t() |> as_tibble() #smoosh them together
colnames(full_count_df) <- c("Dense Human Habitat", "Human Agriculture", "Forests", "Grass and Shrublands", "Rocky, Barren, or Snowy", "Wetlands", "Water Bodies") #label columns
full_count_df |> head() #tada!

#this took two hours
```

# P value calculations
```{r}
#| label: p value calculations

human_hab_count_more_extreme <- mc_df |> filter(Dense_Human_Habitat >= obs_barrow_counts$Dense_Human_Habitat)
human_hab_p_val <- nrow(human_hab_count_more_extreme) / nrow(mc_df)

ag_count_more_extreme <- mc_df |> filter(Human_Agriculture >= obs_barrow_counts$Human_Agriculture)
ag_p_val <- nrow(ag_count_more_extreme) / nrow(mc_df)

forest_count_more_extreme <- mc_df |> filter(Forests >= obs_barrow_counts$Forests)
forest_p_val <- nrow(forest_count_more_extreme) / nrow(mc_df)

grass_shrub_count_more_extreme <- mc_df |> filter(Grass_and_Shrublands >= obs_barrow_counts$Grass_and_Shrublands)
grass_shrub_p_val <- nrow(grass_shrub_count_more_extreme) / nrow(mc_df)

barren_count_more_extreme <- mc_df |> filter(Rocky_Barren_Snowy >= obs_barrow_counts$Rocky_Barren_Snowy)
barren_p_val <- nrow(barren_count_more_extreme) / nrow(mc_df)

wetland_count_more_extreme <- mc_df |> filter(Wetlands >= obs_barrow_counts$Wetlands)
wetland_p_val <- nrow(wetland_count_more_extreme) / nrow(mc_df)

water_count_more_extreme <- mc_df |> filter(Water_Bodies >= obs_barrow_counts$Water_Bodies)
water_p_val <- nrow(water_count_more_extreme) / nrow(mc_df)



#I could make this into a df instead of doing this way huh?

print("P-values by habitat:")
print(paste("Dense Human Habitat:",human_hab_p_val))
print(paste("Human Agriculture:",ag_p_val))
print(paste("Forest:",forest_p_val))
print(paste("Grass and Shrublands:",grass_shrub_p_val))
print(paste("Rocky, Barren, and Snowy:",barren_p_val))
print(paste("Wetlands:",wetland_p_val))
print(paste("Water Bodies:",water_p_val))

#so out of all of these only agriculture is truly significant, but all the '1'basically means the true count was WAY lower than the expected count, which is also significant, and I'll work on that in a bit
p_values <- c(human_hab_p_val, ag_p_val, forest_p_val, grass_shrub_p_val, barren_p_val, wetland_p_val,water_p_val)
p_val_greater_df <- data.frame(habitat = lc_labels, p_value = p_values)
print(p_val_greater_df)

```
